worksheet.title: What Comes First?
worksheet.subtitle: Finding the step that starts it all
worksheet.learning_goal: I can find the step that must happen first.

parts.title: Some steps must come first
parts.text: You cannot slide down before you climb up! Some steps have to happen FIRST. Help Bit find the step that comes first.

parts.title: Watch Bit go down the slide
parts.note: First climb up ⬆, then slide down ⬇. Up comes first.

parts.title: Climb the ladder
parts.prompt: To get to the top, what comes first? Circle it.   ⬆ climb up    ⬇ come down

parts.title: Go through the door
parts.prompt: Bit wants to go through the door. What comes first? Circle it.   (a) open the door    (b) walk through  ➡

parts.title: You try — get ready
parts.prompt: Which comes first when you get dressed? Circle it.   1) put on a sock    2) put on a shoe

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Finding the first step is how you start a plan. If you do steps out of order, the plan does not work.

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Children pick the step that must happen FIRST in a two-step action (like climbing up before sliding down). Knowing which step comes first — and that some steps depend on an earlier one — is key to a correct plan. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper and a pencil or crayon. You read each prompt aloud; the child answers by circling or numbering. Optional: real objects or cards to put in order by hand first.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 15 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). A slide: first you climb up, then you slide down. You cannot slide before you climb.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — climb up comes first.
3. Let them try. Children do Exercise 2 (open the door first), then Exercise 3 (sock before shoe).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — circle "climb up". Exercise 2 — circle "open the door".
Exercise 3 — circle "put on a sock" (the sock goes on before the shoe).

parts.title: If children get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: picking the step they like best instead of the one that must come first. Ask "could you do the other one first?"
Make it easier: act the two steps out and try them in the wrong order — it does not work.
Make it harder: ask for a three-step routine and which step is first (e.g. wet hands, soap, rinse).
Make it active: have children mime the action in the correct order.

parts.title: Ontario Kindergarten link (official wording)
text: Problem Solving and Innovating — children reason about the order in which steps must occur.
In plain terms: noticing which step has to happen first.
No reading is needed from the child — you read each prompt aloud; the child answers by circling, numbering, or drawing arrows.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child circles the step that must happen first in each pair and can say why.
